Food space map · Swedish Food Agency and Fineli databases

Nordic Food Space Map

Foods are first split into the FAO/WHO GIFT nutrition-sensitive groups, which are never mixed. Inside a group, foods sit close when their macronutrients and nutrient fractions are alike (names are not used for this; they only help place new foods): fat (saturated/mono/poly, omega-6 vs omega-3, and the milk-fat C4–C10 marker where measured), sugars (mono-, sucrose, lactose), carbohydrate (starch, sugars, fibre) and protein fractions. Colour by GIFT subgroup or by the clusters found in the data.

What each cluster holds

Median protein, fat and carbohydrate (g per 100 g), the GIFT subgroups inside, and example foods.

All groups

How well the structure found in the data matches GIFT's own subgroups. ARI compares the data clusters with the subgroups (1 = identical, 0 = chance). The other columns give the share of each food's 5 nearest neighbours that share its subgroup: for macros, for fractions, for both together (the space shown above), and for names. Names do not shape the space; they are used only to place a new food, where they find its GIFT group correctly for 82–90% of existing foods and its subgroup for 71–78% (leave-one-out). Many GIFT subgroups are broad ("other and mixed cereals" holds most cereal foods), so data clusters are often finer than subgroups. Click a row to open that group.

Combined only: Country mixing is the share of each food's 5 nearest neighbours that come from the other country, divided by the share expected if country did not matter (1 = fully mixed, 0 = fully separated). Composition mixes well (about 0.8); fractions separate the countries more, partly from real differences (lactose-free milks are common in Finland) and partly from different recording in the two databases, so fine-scale neighbours are often same-country while most foods sit in clusters that contain both countries.

Cereal food tree (treelet transform)

250 cereal foods, each described by macros plus fat, sugar, carbohydrate and protein-fraction mixes. The protein mix (albumin+globulin / prolamin / glutelin) comes from each product's recipe of raw grains. At every level the two most similar foods or branches merge into a prototype, up to a single root. Cut at 8 branches: rice (glutelin-rich), maize, soft wheat breads, wheat buns and cakes, oat foods, and rye with wholegrain flours. Leaves are coloured by dominant grain.

Sources: Swedish Food Agency (Livsmedelsverket), Livsmedelsdatabasen, CC BY 4.0; Fineli, Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare (THL), release 20, CC BY 4.0. Sweden: GIFT groups from the FAO/WHO GIFT FoodEx2 matching table (version 16.2), joined on each food's FoodEx2 base term; 3 foods have no GIFT group. Finland: Fineli has no FoodEx2 codes, so GIFT groups come from a curated map of its 122 food-use classes plus name rules. Fineli measures starch, lactose and individual sugars and gives omega-3/omega-6 totals; it has no C4–C10 milk-fat fatty acids. Protein profiles are recipe-based in both databases: every food is expanded to raw ingredients (Fineli recipes; Swedish raw-commodity recipes) and the curated profiles of those ingredients are mixed by protein weight. Combined view: 6,841 foods; the milk-fat C4–C10 block is left out because Fineli lacks it. Names (TF-IDF on the English food name) are used only to place new foods: they pick the GIFT group and the closest existing foods, and fill in missing detail; the position then comes from the food's nutrients. Composition: protein, fat, carbohydrate and fibre per 100 g. Protein fractions: curated classes for dairy, meat and fish, recipe-based Osborne profiles for cereals; foods without a profile are compared on the other blocks only. Clusters: Leiden on a 10-nearest-neighbour graph, run separately in each group. Layout: UMAP (t-SNE for groups under 15 foods) within each group, so distances between groups mean nothing.
